body:
## Summary

`firrtl-check-comb-loops` crashes on a forceable register whose writable SSA reference is cast to a layer-colored reference and defined as an output probe.

The input passes parsing and verification. No force/release statement is needed, and the design has no combinational feedback.

## Environment

- CIRCT revision: `eade0de61bc5a0d2ba1b9da951b69efcab19f8ce`(HEAD)
- firtool version: 1.158.0
- Platform: Linux x86-64

## Reproducer

```mlir
module {
  firrtl.circuit "Repro" {
    firrtl.layer @Test bind {}
    firrtl.module @Repro(
      in %clock: !firrtl.clock,
      in %data: !firrtl.uint<8>,
      out %out: !firrtl.uint<8>,
      out %probe: !firrtl.rwprobe<uint<8>, @Test>
    ) {
      %target, %target_ref = firrtl.reg %clock forceable
        : !firrtl.clock, !firrtl.uint<8>, !firrtl.rwprobe<uint<8>>
      firrtl.connect %target, %data : !firrtl.uint<8>
      firrtl.connect %out, %target : !firrtl.uint<8>
      firrtl.layerblock @Test {
        %ref = firrtl.ref.cast %target_ref
          : (!firrtl.rwprobe<uint<8>>) -> !firrtl.rwprobe<uint<8>, @Test>
        firrtl.ref.define %probe, %ref : !firrtl.rwprobe<uint<8>, @Test>
      }
    }
  }
}
```

```sh
# Succeeds.
circt-opt repro.mlir -o /dev/null

# Aborts with exit code 134.
circt-opt --firrtl-check-comb-loops repro.mlir -o /dev/null
```

## Expected Behavior

The pass succeeds without reporting a combinational cycle.

## Actual Behavior

```text
llvm/ADT/EquivalenceClasses.h:192:
Assertion `MI != member_end() && "Value is not in the set!"' failed.
```

Relevant stack frames:

```text
DiscoverLoops::addToPortPathsIfRWProbe
DiscoverLoops::dfsTraverse
CheckCombLoopsPass::runOnOperation
```

## Suspected Cause

In `CheckCombLoops.cpp`, the connectivity graph builder matches `hw::CombDataFlow` before `Forceable`. `RegOp` implements both interfaces, so the register takes the former branch and skips `recordProbe()`.

Additionally, `ref.cast` does not establish writable-reference equivalence between its input and output. `ref.define` registers the cast result and output probe, but not the original register reference.

Later, `addToPortPathsIfRWProbe()` calls `getLeaderValue()` for the original reference, which is absent from the equivalence set.

As a control, defining an uncolored output probe directly from `%target_ref`, without the cast/layer block, passes the analysis.
`
title: [FIRRTL] CheckCombLoops crashes on a forceable register reference cast to a layer-colored RWProbe

```firrtl
FIRRTL version 4.0.0
circuit Top:
  public module Top:
    output size: UInt<32>
    wire empty: {nested: {zero: UInt<1>[0]}}
    node sizeNode = intrinsic(circt_sizeof : UInt<32>, empty)
    connect size, sizeNode
```

With normal optimization enabled, this succeeds because canonicalization folds the intrinsic to `UInt<32>(0)`:

```text
module Top(
  output [31:0] size
);

  assign size = 32'h0;
endmodule
```

Running `firtool input.fir --disable-opt ` where optimization is disabled, the intrinsic remains in the IR and `LowerToHW`
reports:

```text
test.fir:6:21: error: SizeOf should have been resolved.
    node sizeNode = intrinsic(circt_sizeof : UInt<32>, empty)
                    ^
test.fir:6:21: note: see current operation: %6 = "firrtl.int.sizeof"(%5) : (!firrtl.bundle<nested: bundle<zero: vector<uint<1>, 0>>>) -> !firrtl.uint<32>
test.fir:6:21: error: 'firrtl.int.sizeof' op LowerToHW couldn't handle this operation
    node sizeNode = intrinsic(circt_sizeof : UInt<32>, empty)
                    ^
test.fir:6:21: note: see current operation: %6 = "firrtl.int.sizeof"(%5) : (!firrtl.bundle<nested: bundle<zero: vector<uint<1>, 0>>>) -> !firrtl.uint<32>
```

`SizeOfIntrinsicOp` is a compile-time-only operation. Its folder computes the bit width from the operand type; it has no hardware lowering. Therefore, `LowerToHW` requires the canonicalizer to have resolved it first. We should be able to successfully compile this without optimizations.
title: [FIRRTL] SizeOf intrinsic requires optimizations enabled to successfully lower

CIRCT mishandles legal consumers of zero-width aggregate values.

The following legal FIRRTL code crashes `firtool`:

```firrtl
FIRRTL version 4.0.0
circuit Top:
  module Child:
    output out: {nested: {zero: UInt<1>[0]}}
  public module Top:
    output size: UInt<32>
    inst child of Child
    node sizeNode = intrinsic(circt_sizeof : UInt<32>, child.out)
    connect size, sizeNode
```

Run with:

```text
./bin/firtool --scalarize-internal-modules=true ./test.fir
```

`LowerSignatures` removes the child instance result because the aggregate has no fields. Its cleanup only handles connects and aggregate projections, so the intrinsic is treated as an unexpected user and the compiler aborts:

```text
unexpected user of zero-width instance result
UNREACHABLE executed at lib/Dialect/FIRRTL/Transforms/LowerSignatures.cpp:419!
```

Relevant backtrace:

```text
#7  eraseZeroWidthUsers(...)                         LowerSignatures.cpp:0:0
#8  lowerModuleBody(...)                             LowerSignatures.cpp:0:0
#9  mlir::detail::walk<mlir::ReverseIterator>(...)
#10 LowerSignaturesPass::runOnOperation(...)
```

body:
Removing the `moore.conversion` op in #11024 has revealed two related gaps in converting between fixed-size and dynamically-sized array types: a fixed-size unpacked array (e.g. an array literal) assigned to a dynamic array has no conversion path, and a plain packed bit vector passed as the actual argument to a DPI import whose formal parameter is a packed open array has no conversion path either.

```systemverilog
string strArr[] = { "hello", "sad", "world" };
```
```
error: unsupported conversion from '!moore.uarray<3 x string>' to '!moore.open_uarray<string>'
```

```systemverilog
import "DPI-C" function void packed_bits_fn(input bit [] data);
bit [7:0] pdata;
packed_bits_fn(pdata);
```
```
error: unsupported conversion from '!moore.i8' to '!moore.open_array<i1>'
```

For the first case, there's no op to build an open unpacked array from element values or from a fixed-size array value — `OpenUArrayCreateOp` only allocates an array of a given size (`new[N]`). Queues have an analogous, working conversion (`QueueFromUnpackedArrayOp`) that a dynamic-array equivalent could follow.

For the second case, MooreToCore's DPI open-array cast support only recognizes array-typed sources, not a plain packed bit vector, and `OpenArrayType`/`OpenUnpackedArrayType` lower to opaque LLVM pointers with no static width, so there's no bitcast to fall back on. A real fix needs to materialize a properly-sized open-array value from the packed operand (allocate and populate it), not just reinterpret bits. This is essentially #11025.
title: [Moore] Missing conversions to open array types

body:
#11024 removed support for casting a fixed-size array to a DPI open-array parameter of matching element type, e.g. binding a `byte data[8]` actual to a `byte data[]` parameter in a DPI function. Test coverage for this was dropped from

- `test/Conversion/MooreToCore/dpi-open-array.mlir`
- `test/Conversion/MooreToCore/moore-dpi-call-lowering.mlir`
- `test/Conversion/MooreToCore/errors.mlir`

This was originally added by @pscabot in #9882. With the `moore.conversion` op gone, we'll need a dedicated conversion op to support this case again.

body:
This was extracted from some detailed discussions with @dtzSiFive on: https://github.com/chipsalliance/firrtl-spec/pull/380

There was a realization that the use of the `emitConnect` function to expand connects in the FIRRTL parser will cause circuits to be accepted which the spec disallows (or always intended to disallow, but may require the clarifications in https://github.com/chipsalliance/firrtl-spec/pull/380).

Consider the following:

``` firrtl
FIRRTL version 7.0.0
circuit Foo:
  public module Foo:
    input a: { flip b: UInt<1> }
    wire w: { flip b: UInt<1> }
    invalidate w
    connect a, w
```

This is parsed into the following:

``` mlir
firrtl.circuit "Foo" {
  firrtl.module @Foo(in %a: !firrtl.bundle<b flip: uint<1>>) {
    %w = firrtl.wire : !firrtl.bundle<b flip: uint<1>>
    %0 = firrtl.subfield %w[b] : !firrtl.bundle<b flip: uint<1>>
    %invalid_ui1 = firrtl.invalidvalue : !firrtl.uint<1>
    firrtl.matchingconnect %0, %invalid_ui1 : !firrtl.uint<1>
    %1 = firrtl.subfield %a[b] : !firrtl.bundle<b flip: uint<1>>
    %2 = firrtl.subfield %w[b] : !firrtl.bundle<b flip: uint<1>>
    firrtl.matchingconnect %2, %1 : !firrtl.uint<1>
  }
}
```

However, this can be rewritten into:

``` mlir
firrtl.circuit "Foo" {
  firrtl.module @Foo(in %a: !firrtl.bundle<b flip: uint<1>>) {
    %w = firrtl.wire : !firrtl.bundle<b flip: uint<1>>
    %0 = firrtl.subfield %w[b] : !firrtl.bundle<b flip: uint<1>>
    %invalid_ui1 = firrtl.invalidvalue : !firrtl.uint<1>
    firrtl.matchingconnect %0, %invalid_ui1 : !firrtl.uint<1>
    firrtl.connect %a, %w : !firrtl.bundle<b flip: uint<1>>, !firrtl.bundle<b flip: uint<1>>
  }
}
```

This will then trip verification:

``` console
# circt-opt Foo.mlir
Foo.mlir:7:5: error: connect has invalid flow: the destination expression "a" has source flow, expected sink or duplex flow
    firrtl.connect %a, %w : !firrtl.bundle<b flip: uint<1>>, !firrtl.bundle<b flip: uint<1>>
    ^
Foo.mlir:2:25: note: the destination was defined here
  firrtl.module @Foo(in %a: !firrtl.bundle<b flip: uint<1>>) {
                        ^
```

This roundabout path gets back to the original error that you would get if you tried to compile this with the Scala-based FIRRTL Compiler (SFC):

``` firrtl
circuit Foo:
  module Foo:
    input a: { flip b: UInt<1> }
    wire w: { flip b: UInt<1> }
    w is invalid
    a <= w
```

``` console
# firrtl -i Foo.sfc.fir
Exception in thread "main" firrtl.passes.CheckFlows$WrongFlow: : [module Foo]  Expression a is used as a SinkFlow but can only be used as a SourceFlow.
```

I have several ideas of how this could be fixed (or justifiably not fixed):

1. `emitConnect` could be run in a mode where it verifies what it is doing before it does it,
2. the use of `emitConnect` could be purged from the parser and instead the connect expansion is moved to a separate pass,
3. or this is "reasonable" under a justification that `firtool` accepts _more_ than what is allowed in the FIRRTL specification.

``` firrtl
    "target": "~|Foo"

    "class":"sifive.enterprise.firrtl.InjectDUTHierarchyAnnotation",
```

body:
Arcilator currently receives `sv.xmr.ref` and `hw.hierpath` from FIRRTLToHW for FIRRTL probe semantics. The existing `arc-resolve-xmr` pass handles a restricted read-only subset by boring referenced signals through module ports and replacing XMR reads with ordinary SSA values.

However, it is unclear whether this is intended to be the long-term architecture or only a compatibility path.

A major limitation is bind-context XMR. FIRRTL-generated `sv.bind` operations are commonly guarded by `sv.ifdef`, while `arc-resolve-xmr` currently only supports unconditional binds. Resolving these cases generally requires first evaluating the SV conditional configuration to determine which bind instances exist.

This means that fully supporting the current FIRRTLToHW output may require Arcilator to implement a configuration-aware SV preprocessing or elaboration stage before resolving XMRs. This seems undesirable for a non-SV backend, especially since the original probe, layer, and conditional-presence semantics were available before lowering to SV constructs.

Possible directions appear to be:

1. Keep `arc-resolve-xmr` as the supported boundary and extend Arcilator with SV conditional-processing semantics.
2. Eliminate probes earlier using `ProbesToSignals`, provided it can become load-bearing for modern Chisel designs.
3. Preserve probes through a non-SV Core-level representation and lower them separately to SV XMRs or explicit HW ports.

The ongoing Probe dialect RFC and #10818 explore the third direction, but this issue is not intended to assume that the proposed dialect must be accepted. The goal is to clarify the downstream requirement even if that proposal is rejected.

It would be helpful to agree on:

* Is `sv.xmr.ref` an acceptable long-term input contract for Arcilator?
* Is Arcilator expected to evaluate `sv.ifdef` and conditional bind topology?
* Should probes instead be eliminated or represented before FIRRTLToHW emits SV operations?
* Which route should contributors prioritize?

Related:

* #10096 — `arc-resolve-xmr`
* #10818 — Core-level read-only Probe dialect
* [RFC: A Core-Level Probe Dialect](https://discourse.llvm.org/t/rfc-a-core-level-probe-dialect/91315)

CC @fabianschuiki @fzi-hielscher @seldridge
title: [Arcilator] Define the long-term strategy for FIRRTL probes and sv.xmr.ref

I've been seeing a lot of really ineffective `firrtl-module-externalizer` reductions when running `circt-reduce` on circuits involving FIRRTL domains.  I _think_ I know what is going on, but I haven't fully verified this.

When there is domain information in a circuit, a module cannot be trivially converted to an external module as it must provide domain associations for all external module ports.

The simplest fix here would be to change the reduction to blindly add one input domain port for each domain kind and associate all ports to those domains.

circt-bmc cannot check temporal properties. A verif.assert on an !ltl.property fails to legalize, so only immediate boolean assertions work.

LowerLTLToCore has been in the pipeline since #9735, but it leaves ltl.clock, ltl.delay, ltl.clocked_delay and ltl.concat untouched, so the failure surfaces late at the assert instead of at the unsupported operator. #9722 covers only ltl.delay, ltl.clock and ltl.implication, predates ltl.clocked_delay, and has been idle since March. The example in docs/Tools/circt-bmc.md fails for the same reason. It also came up in https://discourse.llvm.org/t/lowering-from-ltl-to-core/86263 and https://discourse.llvm.org/t/89621 without a tracking issue.

Reproduction, run with circt-bmc repro.mlir -b 6 --module LtlProbe --rising-clocks-only --shared-libs=libz3.so

```mlir
hw.module @LtlProbe(in %clock : !seq.clock, in %reset : i1, in %go : i1, out q : i1) {
  %true = hw.constant true
  %false = hw.constant false
  %0 = seq.from_clock %clock
  %q = seq.firreg %go clock %clock reset sync %reset, %false : i1
  %1 = ltl.clock %go, posedge %0 : i1
  %2 = ltl.clock %q, posedge %0 : i1
  %3 = ltl.clock %true, posedge %0 : i1
  %4 = ltl.clocked_delay %3, posedge %0, 1, 0 : !ltl.sequence
  %5 = ltl.concat %1, %4 : !ltl.sequence, !ltl.sequence
  %6 = ltl.implication %5, %2 : !ltl.sequence, !ltl.sequence
  verif.assert %6 label "ltl_probe" : !ltl.property
  hw.output %q : i1
}
```

A core lowering for the bounded sequence operators would help, or failing that a diagnostic naming the unsupported operator. Is anything in progress beyond #9722, and is extending LTLToCore preferred over handling these in VerifToSMT?

```
  module FPGATarget:
  ^

// -----// IR Dump After InferDomains Failed: firrtl-infer-domains{mode=infer-all} //----- //
```

This is because DefaultTarget and FPGATarget get different ports for domain (FPGATarget/a[1] is not bounded. It's a bit artifitial but it actually pops up in buffer/passtrough choice). I don't think this is fundamentally fixable in the current bottom up style inference so I think the sensible solution is to enforce domain association for modules used for instance choices.

The current domain inference errors can be further improved beyond what was recorded in #10041 and implemented in #10337.  Specifically, while the current version provides information about _where_ a domain came from, it doesn't provide information on _why_ two domains unified.  Consider the following circuit where `Bar` is an incorrectly specified clock domain synchronizer:

``` firrtl
FIRRTL version 7.0.0
circuit Foo:

  domain ClockDomain:

  module Bar:
    input a: UInt<1>
    output b: UInt<1>

    connect b, a

  public module Foo:
    input A: Domain of ClockDomain
    input B: Domain of ClockDomain
    input a: UInt<1> domains [A]
    output b: UInt<1> domains [B]

    inst bar of Bar
    connect bar.a, a
    connect b, bar.b
```

When compiled, this produces:

``` console
# firtool -domain-mode=infer-all circt/domain-error-improve.fir
circt/domain-error-improve.fir:21:5: error: illegal domain crossing in operation between operands b and bar.b
    connect b, bar.b
    ^
circt/domain-error-improve.fir:21:5: note: see current operation: "firrtl.matchingconnect"(%arg3, %0#2) : (!firrtl.uint<1>, !firrtl.uint<1>) -> ()
circt/domain-error-improve.fir:16:12: note: b has domains [B : ClockDomain]
    output b: UInt<1> domains [B]
           ^
circt/domain-error-improve.fir:19:5: note: bar.b has domains [A : ClockDomain]
    inst bar of Bar
    ^
circt/domain-error-improve.fir:14:11: note: input module port B declared here
    input B: Domain of ClockDomain
          ^
circt/domain-error-improve.fir:13:11: note: input module port A declared here
    input A: Domain of ClockDomain
          ^
```

The information provided records the following pieces of information:

1. The top-level connect `connect b, bar.b` has an illegal domain crossing and it correctly identifies what are the two domains, `A` and `B`.
2. It identifies with good names all of the problematic connections and where they live.

However, it critically doesn't provide any information on _why_ the domain inference algorithm is trying to unify them.  Or: the simple fix is that the failing connection needs to have a domain cast added.  However, this is not the correct fix here.  Instead, the fix is to add a domain cast at the connect inside `Bar`.

This is tricky and I don't have a good line on a solution.  However, I have a couple of ideas:

1. After a unification error is found, it's almost like you want to have a way to re-run domain inference, but indicate that these two domains should never be merged.  The hard part about this, is you don't know what should be included in the set of operations that you don't want to merge.
2. The algorithm working bottom-up is the issue and this should work more from known points in the design.  We know when the algorithm starts that `bar.a` and `bar.b` have to be on different domains because we know about the domains of `Foo`.  However, this information is not used in the inference of `Bar`.  If we continue to allow for the `-domain-mode=infer-all` mode of operation, then it's not a strict "top-down" is better than "bottom-up" and it starts to look more like the algorithm works in multiple directions at once based on the known domain information it has.

Both of these ideas view the unification slightly differently where it's more like you have two expanding bubbles of connectivity and you're looking for the points at which they intersect.  Any of those intersections are then wrong and most likely to be the places where uses need to make modifications.  Granted, this may be a function of the examples I'm seeing and not a truly generally property.  I.e., this seems to optimize for the most distant unification points being the identified problems, when theoretically, any connection point could be the issue.

Regardless, the current information is proving insufficient for me (a developer) to use this and it will certainly be too much for a user.  My current loop here is to rely on `circt-reduce` with a number of optimizations that inline or rename things turned off so that I can get a smaller circuit that still has all the same names, but also has the same domain crossing error.

I'm starting to run into issues where the limited support for constants in `InferDomains` is causing domain inference errors.  Consider the following circuit:

``` firrtl
FIRRTL version 7.0.0
circuit Foo:

  domain ClockDomain:

  public module Foo:
    input A: Domain of ClockDomain
    output a: UInt<1> domains [A]
    input B: Domain of ClockDomain
    output b: UInt<1> domains [B]

    node x = UInt<1>(1)

    connect a, x
    connect b, x
```

This will presently fail domain inference due to the use of the node:

```
# firtool -domain-mode=infer circt/domain-constant-expression.fir
circt/domain-constant-expression.fir:15:5: error: illegal domain crossing in operation between operands b and x
    connect b, x
    ^
circt/domain-constant-expression.fir:15:5: note: see current operation: "firrtl.matchingconnect"(%arg3, %1) : (!firrtl.uint<1>, !firrtl.uint<1>) -> ()
circt/domain-constant-expression.fir:10:12: note: b has domains [B : ClockDomain]
    output b: UInt<1> domains [B]
           ^
circt/domain-constant-expression.fir:12:5: note: x has domains [A : ClockDomain]
    node x = UInt<1>(1)
    ^
circt/domain-constant-expression.fir:9:11: note: input module port B declared here
    input B: Domain of ClockDomain
          ^
circt/domain-constant-expression.fir:7:11: note: input module port A declared here
    input A: Domain of ClockDomain
          ^
```

I had originally thought that this could be made to work with an improvement to the constant checking in the pass.  However, this is fraught with difficulty as the constant-ness needs to propagate like a domain.

In the past, there's been discussions of an "empty" or "colorless" domain that may fit here.  Essentially, there exists a domain that things can be put into which can be used by any other domain, but does not unify with that domain.  In the above example, this would mean that the constant one and the node would be put into this domain.  This would then be allowed to be used by both the `A` and `B` domains, but would not unify with them.

The reason for the complication is that this needs to work through things like primops.  The above example is reduced from what I was seeing internally where this was actually:

``` firrtl
when eq(UInt<1>(0), UInt<1>(0)) : 
  ; body
```

Relatedly, any kind of CSE can create problems here, even if they didn't exist in the input circuit.

body:
Consider
```SystemVerilog
module Gadget(input i, output reg o);
  logic r1 = '0;
  logic r2 = '0;
  
  always @(posedge i)  r1 <= 1'b1;
  always @(posedge r1) r2 <= 1'b1;  
  always @(posedge r2) o  <= r1;
  
endmodule
```

When transitioning `i` from zero to one, `o` should (deterministically) become one, since the posedge will propagate through `r1` and `r2`, and `r1` has to have become high for the process writing `o` to be unsuspended.
https://www.edaplayground.com/x/bt4m

Passing this through `circt-verilog` and adding an arcilator testbench we get:
```MLIR
  hw.module @Gadget(in %i : i1, out o : i1) {
    %true = hw.constant true
    %0 = seq.to_clock %i
    %r1 = seq.firreg %true clock %0 : i1
    %1 = seq.to_clock %r1
    %r2 = seq.firreg %true clock %1 : i1
    %2 = seq.to_clock %r2
    %o = seq.firreg %r1 clock %2 : i1
    hw.output %o : i1
  }
  
  func.func @entry() {
    %zero = hw.constant 0 : i1
    %one = hw.constant 1 : i1
    %tstep = hw.constant 0 : i64
    arc.sim.instantiate @Gadget as %model {
      arc.sim.set_input %model, "i" = %zero : i1, !arc.sim.instance<@Gadget>
      arc.sim.step %model by %tstep : !arc.sim.instance<@Gadget>
      arc.sim.set_input %model, "i" = %one : i1, !arc.sim.instance<@Gadget>
      arc.sim.step %model by %tstep : !arc.sim.instance<@Gadget>
      %o = arc.sim.get_port %model, "o" : i1, !arc.sim.instance<@Gadget>
      arc.sim.emit "o", %o : i1
    }
    return
  }
```
And running it yields:
```
o = 0
```

This is because Arcilator currently uses a different time model ("old" vs. "new" in LowerState) for clock inputs vs. data inputs on registers. Clock signals propagate immediately, while data signals are delayed. This allows it to detect an edge on `%r2` while the `%r1` on the data input still evaluates to zero.

There is a signal race condition in the core IR and it is unclear whether we consider the Arcilator behavior a valid refinement of it. But if we do, the core IR is not a correct lowering of the SV input.

`circt-opt --canonicalize` can turn verifier-clean FIRRTL IR into invalid IR when a FIRRTL canonicalization pattern changes operand constness but reuses a stale result type from the original operation.

I reproduced this on a clean checkout of current `main`, without local changes. The inputs below all verify before canonicalization, but fail verification after `--canonicalize`.

This appears related to https://github.com/llvm/circt/issues/9611. The `mux/pad` cases reproduce the same `firrtl.pad` verifier failure shape on current `main`. The `firrtl.cat` case appears to be a second instance of the same stale-result-type pattern.

Reproduced commit:
``` text
e272897aa [ESI][Runtime] Fix engine teardown oversight (#10785)
```

`--canonicalize` should preserve verifier-clean FIRRTL IR. If a FIRRTL fold rewrites operands or inserts a new primitive op, the replacement op result type should agree with the op's inferred return type, including constness. The three test cases below all verify with plain `circt-opt`, but fail verification after `circt-opt --canonicalize`.

## Case 1: `firrtl.cat`

```mlir
// name: cat-of-constant.mlir
firrtl.circuit "Top" {
  firrtl.module @Top(in %x: !firrtl.const.uint<4>, out %out: !firrtl.const.uint<8>) {
    %c0 = firrtl.constant 0 : !firrtl.const.uint<1>
    %c1 = firrtl.constant 1 : !firrtl.const.uint<3>
    %cat = firrtl.cat %c0, %c1, %x : (!firrtl.const.uint<1>, !firrtl.const.uint<3>, !firrtl.const.uint<4>) -> !firrtl.const.uint<8>
    firrtl.matchingconnect %out, %cat : !firrtl.const.uint<8>
  }
}
```

Command:
```bash
circt-opt --canonicalize cat-of-constant.mlir
```

Actual error:
```text
cat-of-constant.mlir:11:12: error: 'firrtl.cat' op inferred type(s) '!firrtl.uint<8>' are incompatible with return type(s) of operation '!firrtl.const.uint<8>'
    %cat = firrtl.cat %c0, %c1, %x : (!firrtl.const.uint<1>, !firrtl.const.uint<3>, !firrtl.const.uint<4>) -> !firrtl.const.uint<8>
           ^
cat-of-constant.mlir:11:12: error: 'firrtl.cat' op failed to infer returned types
    %cat = firrtl.cat %c0, %c1, %x : (!firrtl.const.uint<1>, !firrtl.const.uint<3>, !firrtl.const.uint<4>) -> !firrtl.const.uint<8>
           ^
cat-of-constant.mlir:11:12: note: see current operation: %1 = "firrtl.cat"(%0, %arg0) : (!firrtl.uint<4>, !firrtl.const.uint<4>) -> !firrtl.const.uint<8>
```

The input `cat` is valid because all operands are `const`. During canonicalization, the adjacent constants are folded into a new non-const
constant value, so the replacement `cat` operands are no longer all `const`. However, the replacement `cat` still has the old `!firrtl.const.uint<8>` result
type.

## Case 2: `firrtl.mux` high arm padded from const input

```mlir
// name: mux-pad-high.mlir
firrtl.circuit "Top" {
  firrtl.module @Top(in %sel: !firrtl.uint<1>, in %x: !firrtl.const.uint<2>, in %y: !firrtl.uint<12>, out %out: !firrtl.uint<12>) {
    %mux = firrtl.mux(%sel, %x, %y) : (!firrtl.uint<1>, !firrtl.const.uint<2>, !firrtl.uint<12>) -> !firrtl.uint<12>
    firrtl.matchingconnect %out, %mux : !firrtl.uint<12>
  }
}
```

Command:

```bash
circt-opt --canonicalize mux-pad-high.mlir
```

Actual error:

```text
mux-pad-high.mlir:11:12: error: 'firrtl.pad' op inferred type(s) '!firrtl.const.uint<12>' are incompatible with return type(s) of operation '!firrtl.uint<12>'
    %mux = firrtl.mux(%sel, %x, %y) : (!firrtl.uint<1>, !firrtl.const.uint<2>, !firrtl.uint<12>) -> !firrtl.uint<12>
           ^
mux-pad-high.mlir:11:12: error: 'firrtl.pad' op failed to infer returned types
    %mux = firrtl.mux(%sel, %x, %y) : (!firrtl.uint<1>, !firrtl.const.uint<2>, !firrtl.uint<12>) -> !firrtl.uint<12>
           ^
mux-pad-high.mlir:11:12: note: see current operation: %0 = "firrtl.pad"(%arg1) <{amount = 12 : i32}> : (!firrtl.const.uint<2>) -> !firrtl.uint<12>
```

## Case 3: `firrtl.mux` low arm padded from const input

```mlir
// name: mux-pad-low.mlir
firrtl.circuit "Top" {
  firrtl.module @Top(in %sel: !firrtl.uint<1>, in %x: !firrtl.uint<12>, in %y: !firrtl.const.uint<2>, out %out: !firrtl.uint<12>) {
    %mux = firrtl.mux(%sel, %x, %y) : (!firrtl.uint<1>, !firrtl.uint<12>, !firrtl.const.uint<2>) -> !firrtl.uint<12>
    firrtl.matchingconnect %out, %mux : !firrtl.uint<12>
  }
}
```

Command:

```bash
circt-opt --canonicalize mux-pad-low.mlir
```

Actual error:

```text
mux-pad-low.mlir:5:12: error: 'firrtl.pad' op inferred type(s) '!firrtl.const.uint<12>' are incompatible with return type(s) of operation '!firrtl.uint<12>'
    %mux = firrtl.mux(%sel, %x, %y) : (!firrtl.uint<1>, !firrtl.uint<12>, !firrtl.const.uint<2>) -> !firrtl.uint<12>
           ^
mux-pad-low.mlir:5:12: error: 'firrtl.pad' op failed to infer returned types
    %mux = firrtl.mux(%sel, %x, %y) : (!firrtl.uint<1>, !firrtl.uint<12>, !firrtl.const.uint<2>) -> !firrtl.uint<12>
           ^
mux-pad-low.mlir:5:12: note: see current operation: %0 = "firrtl.pad"(%arg2) <{amount = 12 : i32}> : (!firrtl.const.uint<2>) -> !firrtl.uint<12>
```

In both mux cases, the mux itself is valid as non-const because `%sel` is non-const. The canonicalizer pads the narrow const arm, but the inserted
`firrtl.pad` is created with the non-const mux result type. `PadPrimOp` inference preserves input constness, so the inferred result is `!firrtl.const.uint<12>`, not `!firrtl.uint<12>`.

## Possible source locations

At commit `e272897aa`:

- `lib/Dialect/FIRRTL/FIRRTLFolds.cpp:1510`: `CatOfConstant` creates the
  replacement `CatPrimOp` with `cat.getType()`.
- `lib/Dialect/FIRRTL/FIRRTLFolds.cpp:1902`: `MuxPad` creates `PadPrimOp` with
  `mux.getType()`.
- `lib/Dialect/FIRRTL/FIRRTLOps.cpp:5716`: `CatPrimOp::inferReturnType`
  makes the cat result const only if all operands are const.
- `lib/Dialect/FIRRTL/FIRRTLOps.cpp:6121`: `PadPrimOp::inferReturnType`
  preserves input constness.

Build CIRCT with -DCIRCT_CADICAL_ENABLED=On.

```mlir
    %0 = synth.aig.and_inv %a, not %a : i1
    %1 = synth.aig.and_inv %0 : i1
    hw.output %1 : i1
  }
```

%0/%1 should be replaced with choices with constants (or simply constants).
Currently they are not folded if there is no constant. 
The easiest implementation would be to check if there is constant zero/one, and if not, we can simply create them before running FR.
